name: RAW
description: RAW is Taiwan's most internationally celebrated restaurant and the one that most clearly announced the arrival of Taiwanese fine dining as a serious force in Asian gastronomy. Chef André Chiang—also the force behind Jaan par André in Singapore—opened RAW in Taipei with a specific mandate: to celebrate Taiwan's extraordinary agricultural biodiversity and culinary heritage through the lens of contemporary fine dining technique. The results have been remarkable. RAW's seasonal menu changes completely every six to eight weeks, each iteration built around a theme drawn from Taiwanese culture, seasonal ingredients, or a specific regional culinary tradition. The cooking is technically impeccable—Chiang's French training is visible in every sauce and every presentation—but the heart of every dish is unmistakably Taiwanese.
reviewSummary: Taiwan's greatest restaurant—RAW's seasonal menus celebrating Taiwanese ingredients through Michelin-level technique have made it Asia's most important advocate for Taiwanese culinary identity.

address.street: No. 301, Le Qun 3rd Road, Zhongshan District

spotlight.title: Taiwan's Greatest Restaurant: Dining at RAW in Taipei
spotlight.excerpt: Chef André Chiang has built Taiwan's most acclaimed restaurant around one of Asia's richest and most underappreciated culinary traditions. Here's what makes RAW the most important restaurant in the country.
spotlight.introduction: Before RAW opened in 2014, Taiwan's extraordinary culinary culture—its beef noodle soup, its bubble tea innovation, its night market brilliance, its exceptional produce from mountain farms and coastal waters—had no fine dining voice. The island's restaurants were wonderful, but its international culinary reputation rested almost entirely on street food and traditional home cooking. Chef André Chiang, who had spent years cooking in France and Singapore, returned to his native Taiwan with a specific intention: to take that extraordinary ingredient palette and present it in the context of contemporary fine dining. A decade later, RAW has been ranked in Asia's 50 Best, inspired a generation of Taiwanese chefs, and fundamentally changed how the world thinks about Taiwanese cuisine.

sections.heading: The Six-Week Menu: Taiwan in Every Season
content: RAW's menu changes completely every six to eight weeks—a cadence that is unusual even by the standards of the world's most ambitious seasonal restaurants. Each new menu is built around a specific theme, often drawn from Taiwanese culture, seasonal agricultural cycles, or a particular regional culinary tradition. A spring menu might celebrate the cherry blossom season in Taiwan's mountain regions, featuring mountain vegetables picked at their peak and paired with preparations that evoke the lightness and transience of the season.

An autumn menu might focus on Taiwan's extraordinary mushroom diversity—the island's mountain forests produce dozens of edible mushroom varieties that are barely known outside the country—presenting them in a sequence that moves from delicate to intensely savoury. A winter menu might honour the fishing culture of Taiwan's east coast, building a progression of courses around the species that are at their finest in cold water.

This relentless seasonal specificity means that RAW at any given moment is telling you something precise about Taiwan right now—not Taiwan in the abstract, but Taiwan this week, this season, this harvest.

sections.heading: The Cooking: French Technique, Taiwanese Heart
content: André Chiang trained in classical French cooking, and that training is visible in every plate at RAW: the precision of the saucing, the economy of the presentations, the flawless timing of temperatures, the depth of the stock work. But the spirit of the food—its relationship with fermentation, its embrace of bold savoury flavours, its use of specific regional ingredients with centuries of culinary history behind them—is entirely Taiwanese.

A recent course built around Taiwan's indigenous mochi (glutinous rice cake) arrived as a delicate preparation that honoured both the ingredient's cultural significance (it is a sacred food in several indigenous Taiwanese traditions) and its extraordinary textural qualities. Another course featured aiyu jelly—a gelatinous substance extracted from a Taiwanese fig species found nowhere else in the world—in a preparation that revealed both its cooling properties and its subtle, complex flavour. These are not exotic ingredients deployed for novelty; they are the ingredients of Taiwanese culture, treated with the seriousness they deserve.

sections.heading: Why RAW Matters Beyond the Restaurant
content: RAW's significance extends beyond its own kitchen. By demonstrating that Taiwanese ingredients and culinary traditions could be presented at the highest level of contemporary fine dining, Chiang opened a door that many younger Taiwanese chefs have since walked through. Taipei now has a thriving fine dining scene where it had virtually none a decade ago, and many of the chefs behind that scene have cited RAW as their inspiration.

The restaurant has also changed how international food media and the global restaurant industry thinks about Taiwanese cuisine. Before RAW, Taiwan's food culture was known internationally almost exclusively for its night markets and its bubble tea. Today, it is recognised as one of Asia's most complex and interesting culinary traditions—a richness that was always there, waiting for someone to present it in the right context.

locations: No. 301, Le Qun 3rd Road, Zhongshan District, Taipei 10491, Taiwan

tips: Reservations open on the first of each month for the following six-week period — book immediately.
The menu is entirely omakase; no à la carte is available.
Wine pairings include excellent Taiwanese craft spirits alongside international wines.
The restaurant is a 15-minute taxi from central Taipei; Uber is reliable.
Arrive 10 minutes early — the meal begins promptly.
Dietary requirements must be communicated at booking; the kitchen accommodates thoughtfully.
Consider visiting Taiwan's National Palace Museum on the same day — it is nearby.
spotlight.finalVerdict: RAW is one of Asia's essential fine dining experiences — not because it is the most technically precise (though it is very precise) or the most expensive (though it is not cheap) but because it has done something genuinely rare: given a great culinary tradition its proper voice. Every meal here is a discovery about Taiwan. That is what the best restaurants do, and RAW does it with unfailing grace.
spotlight.author: Taipei Culinary Explorer

name: Shida Night Market
description: Shida (National Taiwan Normal University) Night Market is Taipei's most student-centric and most vibrant street food destination—a labyrinth of lanes near the university where affordable, excellent food of every Taiwanese tradition is available until after midnight. The stinky tofu (chou doufu)—fermented bean curd fried to a golden crisp with a smell that is bracing on arrival and addictive by the second bite—is Taiwan's most famous street food challenge and reward. The oyster vermicelli, the scallion pancakes, the glutinous rice balls—each tells a different story about Taiwan's food culture.
reviewSummary: Taipei's most vibrant night market—Shida's student energy, stinky tofu, and oyster vermicelli are the essential expression of Taiwan's extraordinary street food tradition.

name: The Guest House
description: The Guest House at the Grand Hotel Taipei occupies the most magnificent Chinese architecture in Taiwan—a palatial Qing Dynasty-inspired structure perched on a hill above the city—and serves Taiwanese and Cantonese cuisine of considerable refinement. The setting is extraordinary: you eat in rooms that feel like the dining chambers of an emperor, with carved wooden screens, lacquered surfaces, and views of the Taipei basin spreading below. The Peking duck is prepared in the traditional manner, carved tableside, and served with handmade pancakes and house-made plum sauce.
reviewSummary: The most imperial restaurant experience in Taiwan—The Guest House's Qing Dynasty palace setting and Peking duck are the city's most historically spectacular dining experience.

address.street: 1 Zhongshan North Road Section 4, Grand Hotel

name: Sushi Shu
description: Taipei's most accomplished sushi counter—tucked behind an unmarked door in Da'an District, Sushi Shu seats eight at a single hinoki counter where chef Shu works through a twenty-course omakase using primarily Taiwanese fish supplemented by seasonal imports from Japan's Tsukiji market. What makes Sushi Shu exceptional is its insistence on Taiwanese waters: the local grouper, the Penghu coral grouper, the east coast Pacific bluefin—these are fish of extraordinary quality that Japanese sushi masters rarely employ. The result is an omakase experience that could stand in any Tokyo counter while being unmistakably from Taiwan.
reviewSummary: Taipei's finest sushi counter—Sushi Shu's omakase focusing on Taiwanese waters and local fish produces a uniquely Taiwanese expression of Japan's greatest culinary art form.

name: Addiction Aquatic Development
description: Addiction Aquatic Development in Zhongshan District is Taipei's most extraordinary food destination—a sprawling complex comprising a sashimi bar, a seafood market, an oyster counter, a lobster tank, a BBQ station, and multiple dining rooms, all centred on the finest possible fresh seafood sourced daily from Taiwan's coastal waters. The quality of the fish is exceptional—Penghu spiny lobster, Taiwan abalone, Pacific bluefin tuna at its peak—and the energy of the place, a cross between a luxury fish market and a restaurant, is addictive.
reviewSummary: Taipei's most extraordinary seafood complex—Addiction Aquatic's combination of luxury fish market, sashimi bar, and oyster counter serves Taiwan's finest seafood under one spectacular roof.

address.street: 18 Alley 2, Lane 410, Minzu East Road, Zhongshan

name: Lín Dōng Fāng Beef Noodles
description: Taiwan's greatest culinary contribution to the world may be its beef noodle soup—a dish developed by Sichuan soldiers who arrived in Taiwan in 1949 and adapted their home cooking to local conditions, producing something entirely new: a rich, spiced red broth (sometimes clear, sometimes in the Sichuan red-oil style), braised beef that falls from the bone, and fresh wheat noodles of extraordinary quality. Lín Dōng Fāng in Da'an District serves one of Taipei's finest versions—the red-braised beef noodles here are complex, deeply savoury, and the noodles produced in-house daily.
reviewSummary: Taipei's finest beef noodle soup—Lín Dōng Fāng's red-braised version, with in-house noodles and a broth of remarkable complexity, is the definitive expression of Taiwan's greatest culinary creation.

name: Din Tai Fung Xinyi Branch
description: The Xinyi flagship of Din Tai Fung—the Taiwanese dumpling institution now operating in fourteen countries—remains the most satisfying of the chain's many branches, not least because of the open-kitchen windows that allow you to watch a dozen focused chefs making dumplings with robotic precision: each wrapper 5 grams, each dumpling 18 folds. The xiao long bao (soup dumplings) arrive in bamboo steamers with a thin wrapper that tears at the slightest misdirection of chopstick, releasing a broth of remarkable clarity and depth. Order the truffle version if available.
reviewSummary: The original and finest—Din Tai Fung's Xinyi flagship, with its open kitchen and benchmark soup dumplings, is Taipei's most essential eating experience.

name: Le Palais
description: Le Palais at the Palais de Chine hotel in Taipei Central holds three Michelin stars and the distinction of being one of the finest Cantonese restaurants outside Hong Kong. The dining room, modelled on a Qing Dynasty imperial hall, is magnificent; the cooking, overseen by chef Pau Wai Leung, is classical Cantonese at its most refined. The double-boiled soups—prepared for eight hours—have achieved local legendary status; the roasted meats are among the finest in the city; and the seasonal dim sum, served only at lunch, are the city's most classical.
reviewSummary: Three Michelin stars and Taipei's most refined Cantonese restaurant—Le Palais's imperial dining room and legendary double-boiled soups represent the pinnacle of classical Chinese cuisine in Taiwan.

address.street: 17 Chengteh Road Section 1, Palais de Chine Hotel

name: Raohe Street Night Market
description: Raohe is Taipei's oldest surviving night market and one of its most beloved—a covered street in Songshan District where the crowds begin gathering at 4pm and the cooking carries on until midnight. The signature dish is the bah-wan (Taiwanese pork ball in starchy batter), but the queues are longest for the scallion pancakes, the braised pork rice (lu rou fan), and the giant chicken cutlet—thin-pounded, crispy, and fragrant with basil—that has become one of Taiwan's most internationally recognised street food items.
reviewSummary: Taipei's oldest surviving night market—Raohe's giant chicken cutlets, braised pork rice, and scallion pancakes are among Taiwan's most beloved street food traditions under one covered roof.
